strengths: The paper provides a clean and general framework for online control of nonlinear dynamical systems with continuous state/action spaces, achieving logarithmic policy regret in the horizon and number of models for finite model classes (Thm. 2.1/3.2), packing-number-based bounds for infinite classes (Thm. 2.2), and a √(Np) bound for parametric families (Thm. 2.3), recovering known linear-system results as corollaries.

The 'separation principle' perspective—decoupling best-model identification via posterior/softmax sampling from certainty-equivalent control—is a fresh algorithmic alternative to optimism-in-the-face-of-uncertainty and is well positioned against both the ML (OFU, TS, explore-then-commit) and adaptive control (multi-model, switching) literatures.

The analysis is rigorous and self-contained: the Lyapunov-based telescoping argument (Prop. 3.1 + Thm. 3.2), concentration arguments for the softmax posterior, the packing-based extension (App. D), the Lebesgue-measure extension to continuous parameters (App. E), and the genericity argument for the excitation condition (Prop. F.2, connecting persistence of excitation to controllability) are technically sound and clearly presented.

The paper provides nonasymptotic second-moment bounds on state trajectories (Cor. C.5) and almost-sure finite-time convergence of model identification (Cor. C.6), addressing a concern central to the control community that is often absent in ML regret analyses.

The persistence-of-excitation assumptions are stated quantitatively and are verifiable for linear systems and (via Prop. F.2) generic for a broad class of nonlinear systems, which is more explicit than characterization via Eluder dimension.
weaknesses: Empirical evaluation is very weak relative to the claims. The numerical example is entirely linear (leaky integrators), despite the paper's headline claim being about nonlinear dynamics; no nonlinear system is ever simulated. There are no baselines (no comparison to OFU, Thompson sampling, MPC, or policy-gradient methods), horizons are only 100 steps (far too short to corroborate asymptotic regret scalings), and most plots show single trajectories.

Practicality claims for the parametric setting (S3) are overstated. The theory explicitly notes that the algorithms require a feedback policy µθ for each sampled model, computed via dynamic programming or offline PPO; for the advertised neural-network/transformer parameterizations this is computationally prohibitive, so the O(√(Np)) result is primarily of theoretical interest. The abstract's claim that the algorithms 'are likely to be useful in practice' is only supported on a small linear example.

The logarithmic regret in the number of models hides a strong dependence on the separation constant ce (regret scales as 1/ce): for model classes with close-to-identifiable or nearly indistinguishable models, the constants blow up. The regret guarantee can therefore be vacuous for dense model sets, and the paper does not discuss this limitation explicitly in the main text.

The regret constants involve cα = e^{3c2M} with c2 depending on products of Lipschitz and smoothness constants, so the finite-time bounds may be extremely loose; no discussion of when the bounds are informative is provided.

The realizability assumption f ∈ F is essential and no misspecification analysis is offered (deferred to future work); the benchmark is the steady-state average cost of a single policy µ for f, which is somewhat nonstandard and limits direct comparability with finite-horizon regret results in the literature.

Presentation issues: several typos ('realization realization', a reference to 'Ass. 8' in App. D before it is defined, 'denumerator'), and the distinction between the abstract-level and theorem-level results (Thm. 2.1 vs. Thm. 3.2) requires careful cross-referencing.

strengths: The paper extends finite-sample regret analysis of online control (previously mostly restricted to linear systems, e.g., Simchowitz & Foster 2020, Dean et al. 2018) to a broad class of nonlinear dynamical systems with continuous state/action spaces, via a clean multi-model/certainty-equivalence design with dither-based exploration.

The technical development is coherent and self-contained: the logarithmic regret for a finite model class (Thm. 3.2) is proved with a Lyapunov/telescoping argument plus a concentration argument (Prop. 3.1), and the extension to packing-number-based bounds (S2) and parametric classes (S3) follows a consistent framework, with detailed proofs in the appendix.

The discussion of model-based vs. model-free sample complexity (logarithmic in the number of models) and the explicit persistence-of-excitation condition (Ass. 3, related to controllability Gramians in the linear case, Prop. F.2 for nonlinear systems) are informative and connect learning theory with adaptive control.
The observation that a nonasymptotic second-moment bound on state trajectories (Cor. C.5) can be obtained despite unbounded noise is a nice bridge to concerns from the adaptive control community.
weaknesses: The realizability assumption f ∈ F (the true dynamics are exactly contained in the model class) is strong and central to all results; the practically relevant agnostic case is explicitly deferred to future work. For the claimed application to neural networks/transformers (S3), realizability together with global smoothness of the cost-to-go V, Lipschitz continuity of all policies µθ over the parameter space, and persistence of excitation for all θ (Ass. 6) are unrealistic for deep architectures, so the O(√(Np)) result for 'neural networks, transformers' is significantly overstated.

The regret benchmark is the steady-state cost γ of a fixed policy µ associated with the true dynamics f (Eq. 1), not the optimal policy; for nonlinear f, computing µ requires solving a Bellman equation for f. This makes the 'policy regret' notion weaker than in the standard online control literature, where regret is measured against the optimal policy in hindsight, and weakens the significance of the results.

Key algorithms are computationally intractable as stated (Alg. 2 requires argmin over an infinite function class, greedy covering, and dynamic programming at every iteration), and even Alg. 3 requires computing/computing offline a policy µθ for each sampled θ. The paper acknowledges this but then the claimed practical relevance is only supported by very thin evidence.

The empirical evaluation is inadequate: a single linear time-invariant example, horizons of only 100 steps, essentially single-realization plots without error bars or confidence intervals, and no comparison against any baseline (e.g., optimistic methods, Thompson sampling for LQR, or even plain certainty-equivalent control with a static exploration schedule). No nonlinear example is provided despite nonlinear dynamics being the central motivation. Figures 1-2 also contain typos and unclear labeling (e.g., 'realization realization').

The regret constants are unfavorable (e.g., cα = e^{3c2M}, exponential dependence on M and on problem constants), and it is unclear how meaningful the bounds are in regimes of practical interest; the paper provides no discussion of when the bounds are non-vacuous.

Incremental novelty concerns: the combination of posterior sampling over prediction errors, certainty-equivalent control, and decaying dither excitation is close in spirit to Abbasi-Yadkori & Szepesvári (2015) [2] for smoothly parameterized systems and to Simchowitz & Foster (2020) [46]; the main novelty is the generalization to nonparametric/finite model classes via packing arguments, which is a fairly standard discretization technique.

Several minor presentation issues undermine polish: typos ('automatically satisfies', 'denumerator', 'the powerfull separation principle'), an inconsistency between the abstract's bound O(Nε² + ln(m(ε))/ε²) and the main text, and notation abuse acknowledged repeatedly in the appendix.

strengths: The paper makes a clear theoretical contribution: nonasymptotic policy-regret guarantees for online RL over continuous state/action spaces with nonlinear dynamics, extending results previously available mainly for linear time-invariant systems.

The multi-model perspective and separation principle (decoupling best-model identification from certainty-equivalent control) is a clean and coherent algorithmic paradigm that contrasts with optimism-based approaches, and the logarithmic dependence on the number of candidate models (ln(m)) is a favorable and interpretable scaling.

The presentation is well structured: the analysis is illustrated in detail for the finite-model setting (Prop. 3.1, Thm. 3.2) with a Lyapunov-based proof sketch in the main text and detailed proofs in the appendix, and the extensions to nonparametric (packing-based) and parametric model classes follow naturally.

The paper connects and carefully positions itself relative to three literatures: online learning/optimistic control, multi-model adaptive control, and online switching control, and it articulates precisely where its assumptions are weaker or stronger than prior art.

The treatment of state boundedness (second-moment bounds, Cor. C.5) and finite-time almost-sure convergence of model identification (Cor. C.6) addresses concerns important to the control community, and the analysis of persistence of excitation (Ass. 3, Prop. F.2) provides insight into when the assumptions are generic.

The numerical experiments demonstrate benign transients, fast convergence to near-optimal steady-state performance, and favorable scaling with the number of candidate models (up to 10,000), with reasonable computational cost.
weaknesses: The persistence-of-excitation assumption (Ass. 3/4/6) is imposed on the closed-loop trajectory generated by the very algorithm being analyzed, with a uniform constant ce over all initial conditions, noise realizations, and candidate models. For general nonlinear systems this is a strong condition whose verification is nontrivial; Prop. F.2 only establishes it for small excitation and locally, so the claim that the results hold for a 'broad class' of nonlinear dynamics is only partially supported.

The parametric result (Thm. 2.3, √(Np) regret) requires Lipschitz continuity of the feedback policies µθ in the model parameters and a stability condition (Ass. 5/7) that, in effect, requires the benchmark policy µ to optimize the Q-function. These conditions are verified essentially only for linear dynamics with quadratic cost, so marketing the result as applying to neural networks/transformers overstates the practical scope; smoothness of policies in θ is not realistic for large overparametrized networks.

The numerical evaluation is limited to a single linear time-invariant system (leaky integrators) and only compares Alg. 1/Alg. 3 against the optimal steady-state policy. Despite the paper's central claim being about nonlinear dynamics, no nonlinear simulation is provided, and there is no empirical comparison against any baseline algorithm (e.g., optimistic methods, Thompson sampling, or Exp3-style switching control), so claims of practical usefulness rest on thin evidence.

The S2 result (Thm. 2.2) is largely conceptual: Alg. 2 requires minimizing over a function class, constructing an ε-packing, and solving a dynamic program at every iteration, which the authors themselves admit is computationally intractable. The generality of the 'no-regret for any bounded function class' claim thus comes at the cost of an algorithm that cannot be implemented.

The benchmark γ is the steady-state performance of the policy corresponding to the true dynamics rather than the optimal policy in hindsight; while finite-horizon extensions are claimed, they are not worked out, and the regret is measured against a class of achievable policies, which somewhat weakens the headline 'sample complexity of online RL' claim.

Several constants in the theorems depend on quantities that are hard to estimate or may be large (cα = e^{3c2M} with c2 growing with problem constants, exp(p) factors in the S3 analysis, Lµ from Ass. 5), so the practical significance of the bounds beyond their scaling behavior is unclear.

The comparison of model-based vs. model-free sample complexity (O(ln m) vs. O(m)) is intriguing but only informally argued; no formal lower bound or rigorous separation is established, so this claimed insight remains a heuristic observation.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely difficult and important problem: nonasymptotic, frequentist policy-regret guarantees for online (non-episodic) reinforcement learning with nonlinear dynamics and continuous state-action spaces, a setting where prior work either gives Bayesian guarantees, requires episodic resets, or relies on mixing/linear-representation assumptions.

Clean and practical algorithmic idea: a Hedge/posterior-sampling scheme over candidate models with certainty-equivalent control plus carefully scheduled excitation noise, which decouples model identification from control synthesis and avoids computing confidence sets or optimistic policies (in contrast to OFU-based methods).

Strong and well-structured results: logarithmic regret O(du ln(N)/Delta + du ln(m)/Delta) for a finite model class (consistent with online-learning lower bounds up to log factors), packing-number-based results for general bounded function classes establishing no-regret learning for broad classes (e.g., Lipschitz functions), and O(sqrt(du N p)) for parametric families, recovering known LQR results (Simchowitz & Foster 2020; Dean et al. 2018) as a special case.

The analysis is rigorous and technically nontrivial: Lyapunov/dissipativity-based telescoping argument, concentration analysis of the softmax posterior under correlated data, persistence-of-excitation assumptions grounded in system identification, a genericity result (Prop. F.2) linking excitation to controllability, and relaxation of realizability (App. G).

Meaningful positioning against posterior sampling RL, OFU methods, Decision-Estimation Coefficient frameworks, switching control (improving O(m^{1/3}) to O(ln m)), and adaptive control (asymptotic vs. nonasymptotic guarantees).
Results also address a concern of practical importance: bounded second moments of trajectories (Cor. C.5) and almost-sure finite-time convergence of model selection (Cor. C.6).

Includes numerical illustrations (linear system, nonlinear pendulum-on-cart with MPC-based policy evaluation, scaling to 10,000 candidate models) demonstrating benign transients and small computational footprint, with implementation details sufficient for reproducibility.
weaknesses: The regret bounds and algorithm parameters depend on the separation constant Delta (and ce, ce-bar), which is generally unknown to the learner; the excitation schedule sigma^2_uk requires knowledge of Delta, limiting practical applicability of the stated guarantees (no fully adaptive parameter-free variant is provided).

Setting S2 is computationally intractable as stated (greedy epsilon-packing plus minimization over an infinite-dimensional class at every iteration); the authors acknowledge this, so the result is a learnability guarantee rather than a deployable algorithm, which weakens the practical significance of that contribution.

The assumptions, while standard in control, are still substantial: a smooth cost-to-go function satisfying a Bellman-type/dissipativity inequality (Ass. 1/5/7) that must hold globally in x, uniform persistence of excitation over all trajectories induced by candidate (potentially non-stabilizing) models, and Lipschitz feedback policies; the paper does not fully quantify how restrictive the global-in-x smoothness/dissipativity requirements are for generic nonlinear systems.

Theorem E.1's statement ('for all N >= 2M there exists a large enough p') is confusing: p is the given parametric dimension, yet the statement suggests p must be large; the constant-dependence of epsilon^2 on unknown quantities also raises implementability questions.

Empirical evaluation is illustrative rather than comparative: no baselines (e.g., Thompson sampling variants, optimistic methods, or switching-control approaches) are compared, and the experiments are on small-scale academic systems; claims about practical usefulness therefore rest mainly on simplicity rather than demonstrated superiority.

The guarantee in S1 becomes vacuous when candidate models are nearly indistinguishable (Delta small); although the paper notes Thm. 2.2/2.3 capture this regime, the finite-class logarithmic result is weakest exactly where the model class is richest.

Some minor presentation issues: typos ('denumerator'), inconsistent constant naming (c_e vs. Delta between Ass. 3 and the experiments), and the regret bound for S1 stated with mixed constants across Thm. 2.1 and Thm. 3.2 require careful cross-referencing.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and genuinely difficult problem: nonasymptotic, frequentist policy-regret guarantees for online (non-episodic) RL with nonlinear dynamics and continuous state-action spaces, where most prior guarantees are either Bayesian, episodic, or linear.

The core proof technique is clean and elegant: combining Hedge-style posterior updates over candidate models with a Lyapunov/dissipativity argument on the cost-to-go function V, yielding logarithmic regret in the finite-model setting and recovering known LQR rates (√(du N p)) as a special case.

The three-tier structure (finite model set, general bounded function class via packing numbers, parametric families) gives a coherent picture of how model-class complexity enters the regret, connecting system identification (persistence of excitation) with online learning.

The separation of model identification from certainty-equivalent control is practically attractive: it avoids computing confidence sets and optimistic policies, and integrates naturally with MPC/PPO, as illustrated by the pendulum-on-a-cart experiment.

The appendix is detailed, with proofs that appear largely self-contained and careful (concentration argument in Lemma C.2, telescoping argument in Lemma C.4, finite-time convergence and second-moment bounds).
weaknesses: The practical applicability of the main results is questionable: the exploration schedule σ²_uk in Prop. 3.1/Thm. 3.2 explicitly depends on Δ, the unknown model-separation constant, which the learner cannot know. The claim that the algorithms are 'likely to be useful in practice' is thus only supported by the empirical section, where the schedule is set from the theorem using known constants.

The persistence-of-excitation assumptions (Ass. 3, 4, 6) are strong and essentially unverifiable a priori: Ass. 3 must hold along trajectories generated by any candidate policy, with a uniform lower bound Δσ²_u. While the authors argue these are weaker than mixing assumptions, the burden of the main results rests on assumptions whose satisfaction for the claimed broad nonlinear classes is not fully established (Prop. F.2 covers only a limited noise-free/linearized setting).

The claims about neural networks and transformers in Thm. 2.3 are overclaimed: the analysis requires a smooth cost-to-go function with uniform smoothness constants (Ass. 2, 7) and a uniform excitation lower bound (Ass. 6) over the entire parameter ball, which is highly questionable for overparametrized neural architectures. The paper presents no evidence that these assumptions hold in any nontrivial deep-learning setting.

The S2 result, while general, is of limited value: the algorithm is admittedly computationally intractable (greedy covering over a function class plus dynamic programming each iteration), and for Lipschitz function classes the packing-number bound yields regret scaling like N^{(dx+du)/(dx+du+2)}, which is barely sublinear and only √N-like in dimension one. The theoretical completeness here comes at the cost of practical relevance.

The empirical evaluation is weak for a top-tier venue: only two illustrative simulations, no comparison against any baseline (e.g., Thompson sampling with resampling, optimistic methods, or robust adaptive control), no ablation on the excitation schedule or the choice of η and M, and all experiments are small-scale. The regret guarantees are never quantitatively validated.

There are presentation and consistency issues that suggest insufficient polish: in Thm. 3.2 the constant cr1 is defined in terms of cr2, which is defined afterwards (circular in statement); Lemma C.3's statement contains typos (unbalanced parentheses in E[V(f(x,µi(x)+nu)]); the experiments in App. B.1.2 are labeled 'Setting S2' but actually implement Alg. 3 (parametric S3); the theorem statement in Thm. 3.2 references constants 'co, c2' that are never defined under those names.

The claimed optimality ('optimal up to logarithmic factors') rests on lower bounds from online regression (Rakhlin & Sridharan, 2014); the transfer of these lower bounds to the non-episodic control setting with dependent data and policy regret is asserted but not demonstrated, so the optimality claim is stronger than the evidence.

Compared to the Decision-Estimation Coefficient framework (Foster et al., 2021/2023), the positioning is somewhat vague: the authors assert DEC 'does not directly handle' dependent states/stability, but provide no formal reduction or comparison showing that the proposed bounds are not achievable (or are worse) within that framework. This weakens the significance argument for the new complexity characterization.

Relative to the authors' own prior work on finite-set model identification (Chatzikiriakos & Iannelli, 2024), the finite-model setting (S1) appears largely an extension of known ideas (posterior sampling + excitation + certainty equivalence) to regret analysis; the genuinely new elements (S2/S3) are the parts with the weakest practical grounding.

strengths: The paper makes a significant theoretical contribution: it provides the first (to my knowledge) suite of nonasymptotic frequentist policy-regret guarantees for online, non-episodic RL with nonlinear dynamics and continuous state-action spaces, covering finite, nonparametric (packing-number), and parametric model classes.

The results are close to tight: the O(du ln(m)) bound for finite model sets and the O(sqrt(du N p)) bound for parametric classes match known lower bounds up to constants, and the linear-dynamics specialization recovers established LQR results (Dean et al., Simchowitz & Foster).

The analysis is technically interesting and largely self-contained: it combines Hedge-type updates, Lyapunov/dissipativity arguments, and a posterior-sampling (certainty-equivalent) scheme, with persistence-of-excitation assumptions that are standard in system identification and weaker than mixing conditions in prior work.

Additional results strengthen the paper's value beyond the main regret bounds: closed-loop second-moment bounds (Cor. C.5), a.s. finite-time convergence of the model estimate (Cor. C.6), a genericity result for the excitation assumption (Prop. F.2), and a clean relaxation of the realizability assumption (App. G).

Numerical experiments (LQR with up to 10,000 candidate models, and a realistic pendulum-on-a-cart swing-up with MPC-based policy evaluation) demonstrate benign transients, rapid posterior convergence, and practical scalability, addressing the common concern that theory-driven RL algorithms are impractical.
The writing is generally clear; the main text gives an accessible summary of the analysis while full proofs are deferred to a detailed appendix.
weaknesses: Assumptions are substantial: realizability (f in F), smooth cost-to-go functions satisfying a Bellman/dissipation inequality, Lipschitz policies, and persistence of excitation (Ass. 3-7). While individually motivated, verifying these jointly for a given nonlinear system is nontrivial, and the class of systems where all assumptions hold simultaneously is not fully characterized.

The regret bound for S1 depends on the separation constant Delta, which can be small and is assumed rather than controlled; footnote 1 partially addresses this but the practical sensitivity to Delta is not explored empirically.

The S2 setting is largely of theoretical interest only: the online greedy packing, minimization over F, and per-iteration dynamic programming are acknowledged as computationally intractable, so only regret (learnability) guarantees are given.

Experimental comparison is limited to the proposed algorithms; there are no head-to-head comparisons against prior methods (e.g., Exp3-style switching control, optimistic methods, or Xu et al.), so the claimed practical advantages are not directly validated.

Several presentation issues: inconsistent labeling (e.g., in App. B the section titled 'Setting S2' implements Alg. 3, which belongs to S3), typos ('denumerator', 'optimisitic', 'F_k^epsilon greedily adding'), and regret plots that show stabilized (constant) regret over a short horizon rather than illustrating the predicted asymptotic scaling.

The policy benchmark is steady-state (gamma_i) rather than the optimal finite-horizon policy; the authors argue the extension is straightforward, but formal statements for that benchmark are not provided.
